places.name: Lạc Hà Tông
places.look: The road climbs a low swell of steppe to a sect (tông môn) of long ochre earth terraces and rose-tiled halls, every one of them turned to the west. On the westernmost terrace stands the Sunset Ring, a great round stone gate with no doors and no wall, through which the whole sect watches the sun go down each evening. Below, the river shoals of Hạc Đinh Thị shine in the low light.
places.lore: Lạc Hà Tông, the Sect of the Drifting Sunset Clouds, is one of the seven great sects and master of the western lands; its arts lean on earth and wood, and its disciples hold the hour of evening glow best for cultivation. The head Tô Vãn Chiếu carries the sword Tử Điện; its twin Thanh Sương fell on Chiết Kích Nguyên in 803, and no one has dared go back for it. The dusk of 803, when the river boats fell silent, is kept each year as an evening of mourning, and the head's youngest disciple Tô Mộ Vân is the sect's brightest hope.
places.history: Nhan Cô Vụ founded Lạc Hà Tông in 290 in the western lands where the sun goes down, and a market soon grew on the river shoals below. In 360 the sect forged the twin swords Tử Điện and Thanh Sương for its armoury. It lost the War of the Pivot beside Tùng Đào and lived under the North Star Compact from then on. Its founder later swore with Phó Tiêu Tương to end the Pivot's oversight; when news of the battle on Chiết Kích Nguyên reached the seat in 803, the fishing boats did not sing at dusk for the first time in six hundred years. Nhan Cô Vụ died in 940 and Trầm Tịch Dương became the second head; in 1160 he stepped down for his disciple Tô Vãn Chiếu, who took Tử Điện. In 1176 Tô Mộ Vân was born on the day the evening glow filled the whole sky.
places.art_brief: A vertical sect seat on a gentle steppe rise, the tallest outline in its land: long stepped terraces of rammed ochre earth climbing toward the west, halls under rose-red glazed tile roofs, and a two-roof pagoda at the crest. The signature element is a great freestanding round stone ring on the western edge of the top terrace, open in the middle, framing sky. Dry golden grass at the base and a single road winding up from the lower left. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, long shadows to the lower right, a faint rose haze over the roofs. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: More terraces climb the rise, a second ring of rose-tiled halls stands around the Sunset Ring, and a covered stair runs down toward the river market.
The terraces crown the whole swell; a tall many-roofed pagoda rises behind the Sunset Ring, and banners of rose silk hang along every terrace wall.

places.name: Nam Phố Đường
places.look: Under old forest near the southern shore stands one long hall whose beams and rafters are painted, end to end, with drifting clouds, so that through the open doors the roof seems to float. Lines of yellow paper hang drying between the trunks, and the smell of cinnabar ink and pine soot carries far down the road.
places.lore: Nam Phố Đường, the Hall of the Southern Shore, is a minor sect of talisman (phù lục) makers and scribes sworn to Lạc Hà Tông, founded in 880 by scribes who painted the clouds of the southern shore. Its hall-mistress Châu Phi Vân, born in Tang Ma Thành, keeps the hall and the maple town and brook village in its care. Every new scribe must paint one cloud on the hall's beams before selling a single talisman, so the ceiling grows a little denser every year. The scribes still wince at the talisman contest of 1190 at Hạc Đinh Thị, which they lost to a girl of fourteen.
places.history: In the Age of First Gates Lạc Hà Tông's founder planted maples on this shore, and the forest here became the sect's quiet hinterland. Through the long North Star Compact, scribes came to paint the clouds of the southern shore and drifted into the habit of selling charms to Lạc Hà's disciples. In 880 they founded Nam Phố Đường as a minor sect under Lạc Hà, and raised the cloud-painted hall. The maple town of Phong Lâm Trấn and the brook village of Hoa Khê came into the hall's keeping. In 930 Châu Phi Vân was born in Tang Ma Thành, and in time she rose to be hall-mistress. When the Ferry War came to the Ngư Ca border, the hall's ward talismans went north with Lạc Hà's disciples. In 1190 its best scribes lost the talisman contest at Hạc Đinh Thị to the fourteen-year-old Tô Mộ Vân.
places.art_brief: A minor sect seat in temperate forest on flat ground near a shore: one long timber hall with upswept grey-tile eaves, its exposed beams and rafters painted with pale blue and white clouds visible under the eaves, a small two-roof gate pavilion in front, and thin lines of yellow paper strung between surrounding broadleaf trees. Mossy forest floor at the base, a path leading out toward the lower right. Warm golden light from the top left filtering through the canopy onto the painted beams. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A second painted hall rises behind the first, joined by a covered gallery, and a walled yard of paper-drying lines spreads under the trees.
A three-roof scripture pavilion with cloud-painted beams rises above the forest canopy, ringed by scribes' cells and a small ink-grinding mill on a brook.

places.name: Hạc Đinh Thị
places.look: Where the river spreads into shallows below Lạc Hà's seat, the market (phường thị) sits on a scatter of sandbar islets joined by plank causeways, its stalls under reed awnings. White cranes stand in the shallows between the islets and do not move for the crowds.
places.lore: Hạc Đinh Thị, the Market of the Crane Shoal, has traded since 320 in the sect's pills, river fish and the talismans of Nam Phố Đường. Cranes are never driven off; a stall a crane chooses to stand beside is thought lucky for the season. A talisman contest is held on the largest islet each autumn, and the market still talks of 1190, when the fourteen-year-old Tô Mộ Vân beat the scribes of Nam Phố Đường.
places.art_brief: A low market cluster on a river shoal in flat steppe: half a dozen small sandbar islets each carrying a few reed-awninged stalls and grey-tile sheds, linked by thin plank causeways over shallow silver water, with tiny white cranes standing in the shallows. Pale sand and reeds at the base. Warm golden light from the top left glinting on the water. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: More islets are joined; a timber market hall on piles stands at the centre of the causeways, and a ferry landing serves the sect road.
The causeways become a raised stone walk on low arches across the whole shoal, with a two-roof market tower at its heart; the cranes still stand below.

places.name: Phong Lâm Trấn
places.look: A walled harbour town among red maples where a river meets the sea, its grey-tile roofs half hidden in leaves. At its centre stands the old Tạ clan hall, its deep eaves lined end to end with the mud nests of swallows, so that in spring the hall seems to breathe birds.
places.lore: Phong Lâm Trấn, Maple Wood Town, grew among the maples Lạc Hà's founder planted around the first hall, and is now kept by Nam Phố Đường. The Tạ family, once great in another land, arrived in 470 with nothing but their name, and the swallows of their old hall followed them; no one in town will knock down a swallow's nest. In 1000 the Tạ and their old rivals the Vương exchanged letters for the first time in four hundred years, and the letter is read aloud in the clan hall every New Year.
places.history: In 295 Lạc Hà Tông's founder planted maples around the first hall, and Phong Lâm Trấn grew among them as a landing where the river meets the sea. Townsfolk still point to a moss-grown stone plinth under the oldest maples and call it the first hall. Through the Age of First Gates and the Age of Seven Seats the town shipped timber and fish to the sect upriver. In 470 the Tạ family came with nothing but their name, and the swallows of their old hall followed them to nest under the eaves of the new one. The Tạ never regained their old greatness, but they became the town's clerks and harbour reckoners. Some four centuries later the new Nam Phố Đường took the town into its keeping, and its scribes began to buy paper and pine soot on the quay. In 1000 the Tạ and the Vương, old rival clans now far apart, exchanged letters for the first time in four hundred years.
places.art_brief: A low walled harbour town inside a rectangular wall at a river mouth on the sea: grey-tile roofs half hidden by red and orange maple crowns, a small timber quay with two boats, and at the centre one larger clan hall whose deep dark eaves are dotted along their whole length with small brown swallow nests. Sea on one side, river on the other, maple woods at the base. Warm golden light from the top left making the maples glow. No text, no people or birds larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: The wall reaches the waterline, a stone quay takes larger boats, and a second clan hall rises opposite the Tạ hall.
A curved harbour mole runs out under the maples, a two-storey gate tower stands on the sea wall, and the Tạ hall gains an upper storey whose new eaves the swallows fill within a spring.

places.name: Tang Ma Thành
places.look: A walled city on a river among endless rows of mulberry and blue-flowering hemp. Its river channels are crossed not by stone but by a lattice of swaying hemp-rope bridges slung between timber towers, which hum when the wind blows. Rope walks run along the outer wall, where long strands are twisted under open sheds.
places.lore: Tang Ma Thành, Mulberry and Hemp City, is Lạc Hà Tông's silk and rope city on the Ngư Ca plain. Its hemp ropes are so strong that Lãng Đào's ferrymen will buy no other, and its rope-makers swear no Tang Ma rope has ever parted under load. The talisman mistress Châu Phi Vân was born here and drew her first talisman in mulberry juice at four; children of the city still paint charms on their doors in purple juice each summer.
places.history: Lạc Hà Tông founded Tang Ma Thành in 330 among the mulberry and hemp fields of Ngư Ca Xuyên, the same year it took the bay of Thu Thủy Loan. Silk from its mulberry groves and rope from its hemp fed the sect's treasury through the Age of Seven Seats and the long Compact. The city lay far behind the front both when Lạc Hà lost the War of the Pivot and when it lost on Chiết Kích Nguyên, and its looms never stopped. In 930 Châu Phi Vân was born here, and at four she drew her first talisman in mulberry juice. By 1100 its hemp ropes were so prized that Lãng Đào's ferrymen would buy no other. In 1174, in the Ferry War, Tùng Đào raiders cut every rope bridge on the Ngư Ca border, and Tang Ma wove new ones in a month.
places.art_brief: A walled city in a rectangular wall on a grassland river: a dense grid of grey-tile roofs, the river channels through it crossed by many thin sagging rope bridges hung between small timber towers, long open rope-walk sheds along the outer wall. Neat green mulberry rows and blue-flowered hemp fields at the base. Warm golden light from the top left catching the rope lines. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: Weaving halls and silk-dyeing yards spill outside the wall, and a stone gatehouse rises over the main rope bridge.
A second wall rings the rope walks and dyeworks, a tall drum tower stands at the centre, and the lattice of rope bridges spreads over every channel, hung with silk pennants.

places.name: Hoa Khê Thôn
places.look: A handful of grey-roofed cottages along a clear brook in open grassland, with wild plum and pear on its banks. Just below the last house a low fence of bamboo stakes crosses the brook, and in spring it catches a pink drift of petals and paper slips.
places.lore: Flower Brook Village has kept a custom since at least 560: every spring, when petals float down the brook, lovers write their names on slips and drop them in together. If the two slips catch on the bamboo fence side by side, the pair are thought bound for life; the village's old women sort the slips each evening and never tell what they find. The village pays its dues to Nam Phố Đường.
places.art_brief: A low cluster of five or six grey-tile cottages along a narrow clear brook in green grassland, flowering plum and pear trees on the banks, and below the last cottage a short fence of bamboo stakes across the brook with a pale pink drift of petals piled against it. Grass and a footpath at the base. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A small shrine to the brook's spirit stands beside the petal fence, and a tea house for spring visitors opens on the bank.
A cluster of inns and paper shops lines both banks, and a covered walk follows the brook down to the petal fence.

places.name: Ngân Than Thôn
places.look: A low village on a gravel bend of the river, its shallows lined with long wooden sluice boxes where flecks of silver glint under the moving water. Heaps of washed grey gravel stand in rows behind the houses.
places.lore: Since 400 the people of Silver Shoal Village have panned the river shallows for silver, which Lạc Hà Tông takes for its coin. Panners work in pairs, one rocking the sluice and one singing the count, so the river here is never quiet. A sluice that turns up a large nugget is retired and hung over the door of the family that worked it.
places.art_brief: A low cluster of grey-tile houses on a gravel river bend in grassland: a row of long narrow wooden sluice boxes set in the bright shallows, small neat heaps of grey gravel behind the houses. Pebbled banks at the base. Warm golden light from the top left sparkling on the water in the sluices. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A weighing house with a sect clerk's office stands at the landing, and a small water wheel rocks the sluices.
A walled assay yard and a smelting kiln with a tall clay chimney stand behind the village, and a stone landing takes the silver barges.

places.name: Phương Thảo Thôn
places.look: A fishing village behind low dunes, where long swathes of golden-green sweet grass are laid out to dry in neat combed rows across the sea meadow. Open-sided weaving sheds face its small harbour.
places.lore: Phương Thảo Thôn, Fragrant Grass Village, cuts the sweet sea-meadow grass that has been woven into the mats of Lạc Hà Tông's meditation halls since 640. Its weavers say a good mat smells of the sea for a lifetime; a disciple who wears one through is sent here to cut the grass for its replacement.
places.art_brief: A low cluster of grey-tile cottages and open-sided weaving sheds behind pale dunes by the sea, with a small harbour of two boats, and a broad meadow striped with long parallel rows of drying golden-green grass. Dune sand and sea grass at the base. Warm golden light from the top left raking across the grass rows. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A fenced mat-drying yard and a jetty for the sect's grass barge join the village.
A walled weavers' quarter with a guild hall and a stone harbour arm shelters the grass boats, and the drying rows cover the whole meadow.

places.name: Thủy Khẩu Thôn
places.look: Where a slow brook mouths into the main river stands a small village of grey roofs beside a dead-straight channel, dug by hand and banked with long ridges of spoil planted with willows. A stone tablet stands where the channel opens onto the river.
places.lore: Thủy Khẩu, Water's Mouth Village, lives on the boat trade where the brook joins the river. In 720 the mouth silted up, and Lạc Hà's disciples dug it out by hand in one winter; the tablet records the cut, and every winter the villagers walk the willow banks and each lift one spadeful so the river will remember.
places.art_brief: A low cluster of grey-tile houses where a brook meets a broader river on grassland: a perfectly straight narrow channel running between two long low earth banks lined with willows, a small upright stone tablet at its mouth. River water and reeds at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the willows. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A small lock of timber gates closes the channel, and a boatyard grows on the willow bank.
A walled river station with a toll house and granary guards the cut, and the channel is faced with dressed stone.

places.name: Ngọc Nhũ Tuyền
places.look: Among grey karst pillars, a stair of milky-green pools steps down a slope, each held in a pale lip of stone the warm water has laid down over the centuries. Steam drifts between the pillars on cool mornings.
places.lore: The Jade Milk Spring rises warm among the stone pillars of Ngư Ca Xuyên's karst, its water clouded like watered jade. Lạc Hà Tông holds it but keeps no hall here: the pillars are full of caves and the beasts that den in them, so the sect sends its disciples to bathe in groups, never alone.
places.art_brief: A natural site, no roofline: a cluster of tall grey karst stone pillars with a cascade of small terraced pools of milky jade-green water between them, each pool rimmed with a pale cream stone lip, thin steam rising. Dark cave mouths at the base of two pillars. Warm golden light from the top left on the pillar tops and the steam. No text, no people, no buildings, nothing outside the place's footprint.

places.name: Thiên Xu Tông
places.look: High on a bare mountain above the heart of the continent, seven terraced halls step down a curving ridge in the bent line of the Northern Dipper, each a little lower than the last. The first and highest, the Pivot Hall, carries a slender black-iron spire that catches the last light long after the valleys are dark. Around the seat the slopes are strangely green for such a height, the mark of the Bắc Thần Phúc Địa.
places.lore: Thiên Xu Tông, the Sect of the Heavenly Pivot, is the oldest great sect and the enforcer of the North Star Compact; its arts lean on metal and earth, and its formation (trận pháp) masters are the finest on the continent. Its head Doãn Ngọc Hành keeps the Bắc Thần Ấn, while the former head Đỗ Tinh Hà sits as first elder. Scented wood from Mộc Hương Thôn burns in the Pivot Hall day and night, beside the old stones of Thạch Kiều Thành's bridge.
places.history: Chung Hoài Cực founded Thiên Xu Tông in 120 under the stars of the Northern Dipper, and the ground around his seat grew rich as the sect gathered, becoming the Bắc Thần Phúc Địa (blessed land). In the Age of First Gates the sect won the ore miners of Ngọc Hành Sơn with fair weights rather than swords and fixed its northern borders for good. It destroyed Cửu Thiều Cung in the War of the Nine Shao, beat Tùng Đào and Lạc Hà together in the War of the Pivot without taking land, and set the North Star Compact at Thạch Kiều Thành. Chung Hoài Cực died in 760 and Đỗ Tinh Hà became the second head; in 785 he named Quý Trường Kích war marshal and gave him the Thiết Mã banner and its tally. Under Đỗ Tinh Hà the Pivot called the Pirate Purge, crushed the rebel Phá Quân Môn and judged one vein war after another. In 1150 he stepped down for his disciple Doãn Ngọc Hành, who became head and keeper of the Bắc Thần Ấn and soon brought the sect into the war at Đan Sơn Mạch on Phượng Minh's side.
places.art_brief: The tallest vertical in the heart: a high bare grey mountain whose curving ridge carries seven stepped terraces in a bent line, each with grey-blue stone halls under dark slate pagoda roofs, the highest terrace bearing a stacked three-roof hall topped by a thin black-iron spire. Unusually green slopes and pines around the terraces against the grey rock of the peak, a switchback road climbing from the lower left. Warm golden light from the top left lighting the spire tip and the west faces of the terraces. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: Covered stairs join the seven terraces, and a walled formation yard with stone array discs opens below the lowest hall.
Each terrace gains a tall pagoda so the Dipper line reads from far off, and a ring of warding pillars stands around the whole ridge.
projects: grand warding formation around the seat

places.name: Củng Tinh Quán
places.look: On a high open shoulder of the plain, beside a round mountain lake, stands a quiet abbey (quán) of low walls and dark tile. In the middle of its main court, on a raised stone platform open to the sky, turns a great bronze armillary of nested rings, green with age, that follows the Northern Dipper through the year.
places.lore: Củng Tinh Quán, the Abbey of the Bowing Stars, is a minor sect of formation masters and star-diviners sworn to Thiên Xu Tông, named for the stars that bow to the pole. Its head Thẩm Bắc Thần keeps the Tuyền Cơ Nghi, the armillary finished in 180, and the abbey reads the Dipper both in the sky and in the still water of Tinh Lạc Hồ; it also keeps the star-iron mine at Vẫn Tinh. In 501 the armillary warned of war and no one listened; since then the star-readers send every omen to the Pivot in writing, sealed, so that no one can say again that they were not told.
places.history: Star-readers founded Củng Tinh Quán on the high plain in 150, a vassal whose very name honours its lord, the Heavenly Pivot. In 155 they found that the high lake Tinh Lạc Hồ holds the Dipper at night as clearly as the sky, and by 160 they were keeping the mine at Vẫn Tinh, where iron from a fallen star is dug. In 180 they finished the Tuyền Cơ Nghi, an armillary that follows the Northern Dipper through the year. In 501 it showed the Dipper's handle turned toward the heart, and the abbey warned of war; no one listened, and the War of the Pivot began the next year. In 789 the armillary went dark for a whole night, and the star-readers burned incense and waited; the War of Broken Halberds broke out the next year. Since then the abbey has served the Pivot as its watchers of the sky, and Thẩm Bắc Thần heads it now.
places.art_brief: A minor sect seat on a high grassy plateau: a compact walled abbey of low dark-tile halls climbing in two short terraces to a raised open stone platform carrying a large green-bronze armillary of nested rings, the tallest element; the edge of a dark round lake at one side. Short highland grass and grey rock at the base. Warm golden light from the top left glinting on the bronze rings. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A second court with a star-map paved into its floor opens beside the armillary, and a covered walk leads down to the lakeshore.
A tall three-roof observation tower rises over the abbey, its open top deck facing the pole, and the walls take in the near shore of the lake.

places.name: Thiên Quyền Thị
places.look: At the foot of the Pivot's mountain, a square market of grey stone halls opens around a tall timber gantry from which hangs a giant bronze steelyard, its beam as long as a boat. Every large sale in the market is weighed on it in public view.
places.lore: Thiên Quyền Thị, the Market of the Heavenly Balance, opened beside Thiên Xu Tông in 200 as a market of weight and measure, and its scales are the fairest on the continent. The sect's standard weights are kept here in a locked hall and brought out each spring to test every scale in the market; a trader whose scale fails is barred until the next spring's test.
places.art_brief: A low market cluster of grey stone halls with grey-tile roofs around an open square on grassland at a mountain's foot, a tall dark timber gantry in the square holding a long horizontal bronze steelyard beam with a hanging weight, the tallest element. Paved square and a road at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the bronze beam. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A second gantry and a covered arcade of money-changers' stalls ring the square, and a stone weights hall with bronze doors stands on its north side.
The market is walled and gated in stone, with a drum tower over the gantries and a long caravan yard on the road toward Thạch Kiều Thành.

places.name: Thạch Kiều Thành
places.look: The first city of the heart sits astride a river in rolling steppe, a walled grid of grey roofs crossing the water on one great stone bridge. The bridge wears its age plainly: its old central arches are dark, almost black, while the wide new deck and outer arches added in 1050 are pale grey. Bell towers stand at both ends.
places.lore: Thạch Kiều Thành grew from the stone bridge where mortal traders from four coasts first met, and is the city where the North Star Compact was set in 510. Its people call the bridge the oldest thing in the heart, and the old stones taken out when it was widened are kept in the Pivot's hall. On the day the Compact was signed every bell in the city rang without being struck, and on that day each year the bells are left silent, so as not to answer. Both the head of Thiên Xu Tông, Doãn Ngọc Hành, and his disciple Doãn Hi Hòa were born here.
places.history: In 50 mortal traders began to meet at a stone bridge here, where the roads from four coasts cross. Under Thiên Xu Tông's protection the crossing grew into Thạch Kiều Thành in 150, the first city of the heart. In 270 Kỳ Tùng Ẩn and Chung Hoài Cực met here and drank for three days, and the Pine and the Pivot kept the peace for two centuries. In 510 Chung Hoài Cực set the North Star Compact before the seven sects in the city and stamped it with the Bắc Thần Ấn, and every bell in Thạch Kiều rang without being struck. On the night the founder died in 760, Doãn Ngọc Hành was born here under the fifth star of the Dipper. In 1050 the stone bridge was widened for the first time, and its old stones were carried to the Pivot's hall. In 1130 Doãn Hi Hòa was born here at sunrise, and Doãn Ngọc Hành took her as his disciple when she was five.
places.art_brief: A walled city in a rectangular wall on a steppe river: a dense grid of grey-tile roofs on both banks joined by one broad multi-arched stone bridge, its central arches dark near-black stone and its widened outer arches and deck pale grey, with a small bell tower at each end. Dry golden steppe and the river at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the pale stone. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A second wall takes in the caravan yards on both banks, and a tall drum tower rises at the bridge's north end.
The city spreads across both banks in a double grid, with a three-roof Hall of the Compact beside the bridge, bell towers on every gate, and stone embankments lined with river barges.

places.name: Mộc Hương Thôn
places.look: A woodcutters' village of steep grey roofs under groves of tall incense trees on a river bank. Low clay curing kilns stand in a row along the water, and their thin blue smoke hangs over the river and smells sweet a long way downstream.
places.lore: Since 600 the scented wood of Mộc Hương Thôn's groves has been burned in the hall of the Pivot. The villagers cut only fallen or dying trees and plant a sapling for every log; logs are cured slowly in the kilns, and a log meant for the Pivot is wrapped in yellow cloth before it leaves.
places.art_brief: A low cluster of steep grey-tile roofs among tall dark-green incense trees on a forest river bank, a row of small domed clay kilns along the water with thin wisps of blue smoke drifting over the river, stacked logs beside them. Forest floor and river at the base. Warm golden light from the top left catching the smoke. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A walled yard of curing kilns and a timber landing for the wood barges stand by the river.
A small walled town of carvers and incense-makers grows around the kilns, with a gate pavilion on the forest road.

places.name: Thụ Âm Thôn
places.look: A village sheltering whole under the canopy of one vast old tree, its roofs dappled and its lanes always cool. From the far edge of the shade, on clear days, villagers can see a grey haze lying low over the plain beyond.
places.lore: Thụ Âm Thôn, Tree Shade Village, lives under its great tree near the edge of the poisoned plain left by the battle of Chiết Kích Nguyên. In 900 a boy of the village followed his goat into the miasma and walked out three days later, grey-haired and calm; the village tells it as a warning, and goats here are tethered to the tree's roots every night. The tree is never pruned, and a branch that falls is burned on the plain side of the village to keep the haze away.
places.art_brief: A low cluster of grey-tile roofs almost entirely covered by the broad spreading crown of one enormous old tree, dappled light on the roofs, its thick roots showing between the houses, a small river at one edge. Forest at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the tree's crown. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A shrine is built into the roots of the great tree, and a walled goat fold and a waystation stand at the edge of the shade.
A small walled town spreads beyond the canopy, with a watch tower facing the miasma plain and a lodge for travellers bound for the battlefield.

places.name: Thần Sa Khoáng
places.look: In the red badlands, a hillside is cut into stepped terraces of bright vermilion spoil, with a shallow washing pool on each step where the cinnabar is rinsed. A low stone furnace house squats at the foot.
places.lore: Cinnabar was found in these red badlands in 300, and Thiên Xu's alchemists opened Thần Sa Khoáng to supply the alchemists' first stone. Miners wear cloth over their mouths and rinse their hands in a stone trough before eating; the old ones say the red gets into your dreams.
places.art_brief: A mine on a red badland hillside: a staircase of vivid vermilion spoil terraces, each with a small reddish washing pool, a dark adit at the top, and a squat grey stone furnace house with a short chimney at the foot. Cracked red ground at the base. Warm golden light from the top left deepening the reds. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.

places.name: Lưu Hoàng Khoáng
places.look: Flat pans of yellow sulphur crust spread across a grey badland floor, broken by steaming fissures, with low stone sheds where the crust is scraped and bagged. The ground around them is stained in rings of yellow, white and rust.
places.lore: Since 420 Thiên Xu has mined the sulphur crusts at Lưu Hoàng for fire powders, and the badlands smell of eggs for twenty li. Workers come in shifts and never sleep on site, and a gong is struck at the sheds whenever the fissures breathe harder than usual.
places.art_brief: A mine on flat grey badlands: shallow pans of bright yellow sulphur crust ringed with white and rust stains, thin steam rising from dark fissures, two low grey stone sheds with flat roofs. Cracked grey ground at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the yellow crust. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.

places.name: Vẫn Tinh Khoáng
places.look: On the high plain, a shallow round crater lined with dark, rust-streaked rock holds a timber headframe and winch over the deepest shaft at its centre. Small stone cairns mark the crater rim.
places.lore: At the end of the Wild Age stones fell from the sky on Thiên Tuyền Nguyên for nine days, and the iron at Vẫn Tinh is said to be from one of them. By 160 that star iron was being dug here, and Củng Tinh Quán keeps the mine still. The abbey's star-readers come each year to sight the crater rim against the stars.
places.art_brief: A mine on a high grassy plateau: a shallow round crater of dark rust-streaked rock with a timber headframe and winch wheel over a shaft at its centre, a ring of small grey stone cairns along the rim, a cart track leading out. Short highland grass at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the headframe. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.

places.name: Tinh Lạc Hồ
places.look: High on the plain beside Củng Tinh Quán lies a dark, perfectly round lake so still it reads as black glass, rimmed by a single ring of pale stones. At night the whole Northern Dipper lies in it, star for star.
places.lore: Tinh Lạc Hồ, the Lake Where the Stars Fall, is a high lake that holds the Dipper at night as clearly as the sky. The star-readers of Củng Tinh Quán read it alongside their armillary, and they forbid boats, fishing and even skipping stones, lest a ripple spoil a reading. Herders believe a wish whispered at the water's edge on a windless night is heard by the stars themselves.
places.history: At the end of the Wild Age stones fell from the sky on Thiên Tuyền Nguyên for nine days, and the herders of the high plain came to believe the round lake was where the first of them had struck. When Củng Tinh Quán was founded nearby in the Age of First Gates, its star-readers studied the lake from the shore. In 155 they found that Tinh Lạc Hồ holds the Dipper at night as clearly as the sky. They set a ring of pale stones around the water to mark where readers may stand, and banned boats and fishing. When the abbey's armillary was finished a generation later, the abbey began to read sky and lake together, trusting a sign only when both agreed. No sect holds the lake itself, but no one has broken the abbey's ban in living memory.
places.art_brief: A natural site, no roofline: a small perfectly round lake of very dark, mirror-still water on a high grassy plateau, rimmed by a single thin ring of pale stones, faint star-like glints in the water. Short highland grass and grey rock at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the stone ring, the water staying dark. No text, no people, no buildings, nothing outside the place's footprint.

places.name: Thương Ưng Đài
places.look: A high flat-topped stone table rises from the plateau, its cliff rim ringed with the stick nests of grey hawks and its top scoured to bare rock by the wind. The hawks circle it all day.
places.lore: Thương Ưng Đài, the Grey Hawk Terrace, is the hunting ground of the grey hawks on the high plateau near Chiết Kích Nguyên. Herders say the hawks will not fly over the poisoned plain, and that the day they do, the miasma is thinning. Young cultivators climb up to take hawk chicks for taming, and the hawks remember their faces.
places.art_brief: A natural site, no roofline: a flat-topped stone mesa rising from a high plateau, its cliff rim dotted with dark stick nests, its top bare wind-scoured rock, a few tiny grey hawks circling above. Scree and sparse highland grass at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the mesa face. No text, no people, no buildings, nothing outside the place's footprint.

places.name: Thối Tinh Môn
places.look: On a steep mountain flank, a sect of soot-dark stone halls climbs beside a stream led through a long cascade of stone quenching troughs, each spilling into the next. White steam bursts from the troughs whenever a blade is plunged, and the whole slope seems to smoke.
places.lore: Thối Tinh Môn, the Gate of the Quenched Stars, is a minor sect of weapon forgers (luyện khí) sworn to Thiên Xu Tông; its smiths quench star iron in mountain water and name their work after their lord's stars. In 600 it forged the halberd Trầm Sa Kích for the young officer Quý Trường Kích, and the forge where it was made is kept swept and cold, never used again. Its head Cát Lưu Quang forged a blade from the star that fell near Thanh Bách.
places.history: Smiths who quenched star iron in the mountain river founded Thối Tinh Môn in 330 under Thiên Xu, and in 335 they claimed the Mine of the Iron from Beyond the Sky, saying its ore fell with the stars. Through the Age of Seven Seats they armed the Pivot's disciples, and the War of the Pivot kept every trough steaming. In 600 they forged the halberd Trầm Sa Kích from star iron for a young officer of Thiên Xu, Quý Trường Kích. Two centuries later he fell as war marshal on Chiết Kích Nguyên and was laid under the Vạn Cốt Trủng with the halberd, whose iron has not worn away. The smiths count that as the proof of their quenching. In 1050 Cát Lưu Quang became head and forged a blade from the star that fell near Thanh Bách.
places.art_brief: A vertical minor sect seat on a steep grey mountain flank: soot-darkened stone halls with dark-tile roofs climbing in terraces, a two-roof forge hall at the top, and beside them a long cascade of square stone troughs stepping down the slope with water spilling from one to the next and white steam rising. Grey rock and a mountain stream at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the steam. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A second cascade of troughs and a walled ore yard open beside the first, and the forge hall gains a third roof.
A tall smoke tower of black stone crowns the seat, and a covered stair runs from the forges down to the mine road.

places.name: Phất Y Cốc
places.look: In a high green valley ringed by grey peaks, a modest sect of plain timber halls stands behind a tall stone gate whose name board is left deliberately blank. Swordsmen pass in and out beneath the empty board without a word.
places.lore: Phất Y Cốc, the Valley of the Brushed Sleeve, is a minor sword sect sworn to Thiên Xu Tông that hires out its swordsmen; its name comes from the poem of the swordsman who, deed done, brushes his sleeve and goes, hiding body and name. Its swords are forged from the ore of Can Tương, as its founder began. Disciples carve their names on nothing and take no credit for any deed, and the blank board over the gate is the sect's only boast. Its head Thạch Tàng Danh fought Tư Không Hạc Niên to a standstill on Cùng Mục Phong in 1130, and will not speak of it.
places.history: In 560 a swordsman who brushed his sleeve and left after every deed founded Phất Y Cốc in this high valley, and dug the ore of Can Tương for its swords. He left no name on the gate, and none has been added since. The valley grew into a sword sect sworn to Thiên Xu, hiring out its swordsmen across the heart through the long Compact, often on errands no sect would put its own name to. In the Age of Vein Wars its blades were wanted on every border, and its swordsmen took pay from either side but, by the valley's rule, never crossed swords with one another. In 1130 its head Thạch Tàng Danh dueled Tư Không Hạc Niên on Cùng Mục Phong for three days; neither won, and Tư Không Hạc Niên left without a sect. From 1131 Thạch Tàng Danh would not speak of the duel, and his disciples began to climb the peak to see the sword marks.
places.art_brief: A vertical minor sect seat in a high green mountain valley: a tall plain grey stone gate with an empty pale name board across its top, behind it unpainted timber halls with grey-tile roofs climbing a short slope to a modest two-roof hall. Green meadow and grey boulders at the base, peaks at the edge of the footprint. Warm golden light from the top left on the blank board. No text anywhere, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A walled practice yard of raked sand and a row of guest lodgings for hiring patrons stand below the gate.
A tall sword pavilion of three plain roofs rises at the valley head, with a stone stair to a meditation ledge above, and still no name carved anywhere.

places.name: Tinh Hán Thành
places.look: Thiên Xu's port on the inland sea sits where a river meets the shore, a walled grid of grey roofs behind a long curving breakwater. The breakwater is the reef itself: a line of great white arched ribs, the bones of the old sea-serpent, rising out of the water with stone packed between them. At night the harbour lamps and the Milky Way in the water make the city seem set among stars.
places.lore: Tinh Hán Thành, the City of the Star River, was founded by Thiên Xu Tông in 260 on the reef left by the sea-serpent a nameless swordsman killed in 15. A city formation (trận pháp) runs along its walls and the bone reef, and formation masters are common here; the freelance master Vệ Văn Cơ was born in the city and drew formations in the harbour sand before he could talk. Wheat comes from the mills of Thủy Đối and pearls from Châu Bạng, and sailors touch the nearest rib for luck before every voyage.
places.history: In 15 a nameless swordsman killed the sea-serpent of the inland sea, and its bones became a reef. In 260 Thiên Xu Tông founded Tinh Hán Thành on that reef as its port on the inland sea, packing stone between the ribs to make the breakwater. Its formation was laid along the walls and the reef against storms and sea beasts, and the Pivot's formation masters have kept it in repair ever since. In the Age of Seven Seats pearl oysters found in the shallows at Châu Bạng gave the port its pearl trade, and in the Compact years the water mills at Thủy Đối ground wheat for the whole city. Ore from Ngọc Hành Sơn and star iron from Thối Tinh Môn came down to its quays and went out across the sea. In 980 Vệ Văn Cơ was born here and drew formations in the harbour sand before he could talk.
places.art_brief: A walled port city in a rectangular wall where a river meets a calm sea on steppe coast: a grid of grey-tile roofs behind a long curving breakwater made of huge white arched bone ribs rising from the water with grey stone packed between them, a few boats moored inside. Sea and river mouth at the base. Warm golden light from the top left making the white ribs glow. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: The wall runs the whole shore, a second stone quay reaches out from the bone reef, and a lighthouse tower rises at the reef's end.
A grand harbour hall with a three-roof pagoda faces the sea, the reef is armoured with dressed stone between every rib, and the formation's pillars glow faintly along the walls at dusk.

places.name: Song Kiều Trấn
places.look: A walled town on the river road where two humpbacked stone bridges cross the river side by side, one for carts going in and one for carts going out, with a small toll house on a pier between them. In the square behind stands a row of open ore scales under a long tiled roof.
places.lore: Song Kiều Trấn, Twin Bridges Town, has weighed the miners' ore on open scales in its square since 235, when Thiên Xu's assayers first did it in public view; no miner of Ngọc Hành has rebelled since. The Ôn clan built the twin bridges in 900 and keeps the tolls, and an Ôn sits in the toll house every day of the year. Locals cross by one bridge and come home by the other; using the wrong one is said to bring a bad bargain.
places.art_brief: A low town inside a rectangular wall on a grassland river: grey-tile roofs, two small parallel humpbacked stone bridges side by side over the river with a tiny toll house on a pier between them, and a long open tiled shed in the square. River and grassy banks at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the bridge arches. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A second wall takes in an ore yard beside the bridges, and an Ôn clan hall with a two-storey gate faces the toll pier.
The town spreads across both banks inside one wall, with a drum tower over the square and a stone assay hall raised over the open scales.

places.name: Thủy Đối Thôn
places.look: A village on a fast stream where a row of waterwheels drives long wooden trip-hammers that rise and fall into stone mortars, thudding all day under open sheds. Flour dust whitens the roofs.
places.lore: Since 700 the water mills at Thủy Đối have ground the wheat of Thanh Mạch for all of Tinh Hán Thành. The hammers stop only on New Year's night, when the village stills the wheels and the silence wakes the babies.
places.art_brief: A low cluster of flour-whitened grey-tile roofs along a fast stream on grassland, a row of wooden waterwheels under open sheds, each driving a long wooden trip-hammer beam over a stone mortar. Stream and green banks at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the turning wheels. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: More wheels and a granary on stone piers line the stream, and a cart yard opens on the road to Tinh Hán.
A walled mill town with a sluice gate across the stream and a millers' guild hall grows around the hammer sheds.

places.name: Thanh Mạch Thôn
places.look: A farming village on a low rise above a river, its houses gathered around a round threshing floor of polished stone on the hilltop, with a heavy stone roller standing upright at its centre. Green wheat falls away on every side.
places.lore: Thanh Mạch Thôn, Green Wheat Village, grows the wheat the mills of Thủy Đối grind for Tinh Hán Thành. Its threshing floor is the village's meeting place, court and festival ground; the stone roller is laid down only for the harvest and set upright again when the last sheaf is in.
places.art_brief: A low cluster of grey-tile farmhouses around a round pale stone threshing floor on a gentle hilltop, a single upright stone roller at its centre, green wheat fields sloping down to a river. Wheat and a cart track at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the threshing floor. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A granary and a shrine to the field spirit stand beside the threshing floor, and irrigation channels run down to the river.
A small walled town with a market lane grows around the threshing floor, and a waterwheel lifts river water to terraced fields.

places.name: Châu Bạng Thôn
places.look: A fishing village on the inland sea whose house walls are set all over with oyster shells, so the whole village glitters white and pearl-grey in the sun. Diving boats are drawn up on a beach of broken shell.
places.lore: Pearl oysters in the shallows gave Châu Bạng Thôn its name in 400 and Tinh Hán Thành its pearl trade. Every diver sets the shell of their first pearl into the wall of the family house, so a house's walls tell how many divers it has raised.
places.art_brief: A low cluster of grey-tile cottages on a flat sea shore, their walls studded with shimmering white and pearl-grey oyster shells, small diving boats on a pale shell beach. Shallow turquoise water at the base. Warm golden light from the top left making the shell walls sparkle. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A walled pearl-sorting yard and a stone jetty for the Tinh Hán boats stand on the beach.
A small walled harbour town with a pearl guild hall grows behind the beach, with oyster beds fenced in the shallows.

places.name: Thiên Ngoại Khoáng
places.look: A sheer mountain face streaked rust-red, with a vertical line of square adits cut one above another and iron chains hanging from each down to the ore yard below. A sorting shed with a dark roof stands at the bottom by a stream.
places.lore: Thối Tinh Môn claimed the Mine of the Iron from Beyond the Sky in 335 and says its ore fell with the stars. Some star-readers quietly doubt it, but no smith who has worked the ore will hear a word against it.
places.art_brief: A mine on a sheer grey mountain face streaked with rust-red, a vertical column of small square adit openings one above another, thin iron chains hanging from them to a small ore yard and dark-roofed shed beside a stream. Scree at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the rust streaks. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.

places.name: Huyền Thiết Khoáng
places.look: Deep in the mountain a single great shaft opens under a massive stone winch house, and the ramp down to the road is worn into ruts a hand deep by carts that each carry one black ingot.
places.lore: Black iron was found deep under the mountain at Huyền Thiết in 280; it is so heavy that a cart carries only one ingot. Thiên Xu works it for armour and array anchors, and the oxen here are bred for the ramp and are the strongest in Ngọc Hành Sơn.
places.art_brief: A mine on a high mountain slope: a heavy square stone winch house over a dark shaft mouth, a steep stone ramp below scored with deep twin cart ruts, a single cart with one black ingot on it. Grey rock at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the winch house. No text, no people or oxen larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.

places.name: Can Tương Khoáng
places.look: High on a steep slope, two adits open side by side in the grey rock, one a little larger than the other, with a small stone shrine between them blackened by forge smoke. A narrow path zigzags down toward Phất Y Cốc.
places.lore: Named for Can Tương, the swordsmith of legend, this is where Phất Y Cốc digs the ore for its swords. The miners call the two adits the husband and the wife, after the legend of the paired swords, and ore from both is mixed in every blade; a sword of one ore alone, they say, will not keep its edge.
places.art_brief: A mine on a steep grey mountain slope: two dark adit mouths side by side, one slightly larger, a tiny soot-blackened stone shrine with a single small roof between them, a thin zigzag path descending. Grey scree at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the shrine. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.

places.name: Bạch Ngân Khoáng
places.look: Below a hillside stained red with cinnabar, a fan of pale silver-grey spoil spills from the adit mouths, so the slope looks dipped in two colours. A walled smelting yard with a squat chimney sits at the foot.
places.lore: Silver was found below the cinnabar slopes at Bạch Ngân in 450, and Thiên Xu's coin is struck from it. The mine lies close to Phượng Minh's border; in the Cinnabar Vein War its miners slept in the adits while the fighting at Đan Sơn Mạch lit the ridge above.
places.art_brief: A mine on a mountain slope whose upper half is red cinnabar rock and lower half a broad fan of pale silver-grey spoil spilling from two adits, a small walled smelting yard with a squat chimney at the foot. Rock and a road at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the red and silver slope. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.

places.name: Thanh Ải Phong
places.look: The highest peak of Ngọc Hành Sơn rises above bare grey ridges, its upper slopes wrapped in a band of soft blue haze that never burns off, so the summit is never seen. Climbers say the haze looks thick from below and is gone when walked into.
places.lore: Thanh Ải Phong, the Peak of the Blue Haze, is held by no sect; its name comes from the old line about blue haze that, walked into, is gone. Those who climb into the haze come down saying they found nothing but bare rock and their own footprints. In 1180 the haze lifted for a day for the first time in memory and a temple was seen on the summit; by evening it was gone, and the paths up the peak have never been busier.
places.history: Since the Wild Age the summit of Thanh Ải Phong has hidden in its blue haze, and the miners of the ranges below never could say what stands at the top. When Thiên Xu Tông took Ngọc Hành Sơn's ore mountains under its protection in the Age of First Gates, the peak was left unclaimed, for there seemed to be nothing on it to claim. Generations of hermits and treasure-seekers climbed into the haze and found only bare rock and their own footprints. The Pivot's surveyors left the summit blank on their mine maps and formation charts alike. In 1180 the haze lifted for a day for the first time in memory, and a temple was seen on the summit; by evening it was gone. Since then cultivators from across the heart have camped below the haze line, waiting for it to lift again.
places.art_brief: A natural site, no roofline: a tall sharp grey peak above lower ridges, its upper third wrapped in a thick soft band of pale blue haze through which the summit is only a faint suggestion. Scree, snow streaks on the shaded side and stunted pines at the base. Warm golden light from the top left glowing on the haze band. No buildings (no temple visible), no text, no people, nothing outside the place's footprint.

places.name: Cùng Mục Phong
places.look: A narrow summit of pale granite stands above the ranges, so high that on clear days the plains and the shine of the inland sea seem to lie at its feet. Its flat top rock is criss-crossed with long, deep sword cuts that look as fresh as if they were made yesterday.
places.lore: Cùng Mục Phong, the Peak of the Farthest Sight, takes its name from the poem about climbing one storey more to see a thousand li further. In 1130 Tư Không Hạc Niên dueled Thạch Tàng Danh of Phất Y Cốc here for three days; neither won, and Tư Không Hạc Niên left without a sect. Thạch Tàng Danh will not speak of it, so Phất Y Cốc's disciples climb the peak to read the duel in the cuts; the summit winds are fierce, and not all of them come down.
places.history: In the Age of First Gates the peak was a lookout for the miners of Ngọc Hành Sơn, who watched from its spurs for beasts coming off the high valleys. Its name came from the old poem, and climbers took up the custom of adding one stone to the summit cairn to see a little further. After Phất Y Cốc was founded in the valleys below, its swordsmen used the summit for their trials, though no sect ever claimed it. In 1130 Tư Không Hạc Niên dueled Thạch Tàng Danh of Phất Y Cốc on the peak for three days; neither won, and Tư Không Hạc Niên left without a sect. In 1131 Thạch Tàng Danh would not speak of the duel, and Phất Y Cốc's disciples began to climb the peak to see the sword marks. The cuts have not weathered since, and climbers say the sword intent left in them still stings a careless hand.
places.art_brief: A natural site, no roofline: a narrow pale granite summit thrusting above darker ridges, its flat top rock scored with a criss-cross of long straight bright cuts, a small stone cairn at one end. Bare rock and wind-bent juniper at the base. Warm golden light from the top left catching the cuts so they gleam. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.

places.name: Vạn Trùng Hạp
places.look: A deep, twisting gorge where the river races white between ranks of steep ridges folded one behind another like stacked screens. A narrow plank road on timber beams socketed into the cliff runs along one wall above the rapids.
places.lore: Vạn Trùng Hạp, the Gorge of Ten Thousand Mountains, takes its name from the poem of the light boat that has passed ten thousand mountains. Boats in the gorge pass ten thousand mountains in a day, and the river is the fastest road to the sea. Travellers going upstream take the plank road; boatmen going down never look back, since a pilot who turns his head is said to lose the river.
places.history: The river cut Vạn Trùng Hạp through Ngọc Hành Sơn long before any cultivator came to the heart. When Thiên Xu took the ore mountains and founded its port Tinh Hán Thành on the inland sea in the Age of First Gates, the gorge became the quickest way to bring ore down toward the coast. Ore boats ran the rapids, and the wrecks of the reckless still lie in the deep pools. By 620 it was said that boats in the gorge passed ten thousand mountains in a day, and that the river was the fastest road to the sea. A plank road was socketed into the cliff for those going upstream, and it has been rebuilt beam by beam ever since. No sect holds the gorge, and its pilots answer to no one but the river.
places.art_brief: A natural site, no roofline: a deep winding gorge seen from above at an angle, white-water river at the bottom between steep layered ridges stacked one behind another, a thin timber plank road on beams clinging to the left cliff wall, a single tiny boat on the rapids. Grey and ochre rock with dark pines on the ledges. Warm golden light from the top left on the upper ridges, the gorge floor in cool shadow. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.

places.name: Thiết Bối Cốc
places.look: A broad highland valley whose rock walls have been gnawed and scraped, so bands of raw ore gleam like polished metal along the slopes. Big grey shapes move slowly among the boulders, their backs plated like iron.
places.lore: In Thiết Bối Cốc, Iron-Back Valley, beasts with iron-plated backs feed on the ore of Ngọc Hành Sơn, grinding the veins out of the rock. Smiths prize the plates they shed, and hunters come for them; the beasts are slow and seldom angry, but a herd on the move will flatten a camp.
places.art_brief: A natural site, no roofline: a broad highland valley with scraped rock walls showing gleaming metallic bands of ore, scattered boulders on the floor and a few small grey beasts with plated backs among them. Highland grass and stones at the base. Warm golden light from the top left glinting on the ore bands. No text, no people, no buildings, nothing outside the place's footprint.

places.name: Xích Viêm Khẩu
places.look: On a bare black cone high in Ngọc Hành Sơn, a wide red mouth glows and breathes heat, its lava cooling with a metallic sheen. A ring of carved grey warding pillars stands around the lower slope.
places.lore: Xích Viêm Khẩu, the Red Flame Mouth, is a vent of the volcano in Ngọc Hành Sơn, and the fire that comes out of it carries the mountain's metal. Thiên Xu holds it and lets no one camp inside the warding ring; its smiths and alchemists come only to draw fire for a single working and leave the same day. Miners below say the mountain grumbles before every vein war, though no one has made it prove it.
places.history: Xích Viêm Khẩu was burning before the first cultivators came to the heart, and the miners of Ngọc Hành Sơn called it the red mouth long before it had a written name. When Thiên Xu Tông took the ore mountains under its protection in the Age of First Gates, it took the vent with them. Its formation masters raised a ring of warding pillars on the lower slope to keep the vent's fire from the mines and the miners from the fire. Through the Age of Seven Seats the sect's smiths and alchemists drew fire here for workings that needed metal and flame together. After Chúc Long Sơn erupted under the ice and buried Hồ Thiên Phái in the Age of Seven Seats, the Pivot set permanent wardens at Xích Viêm, and the pillars have been kept in repair ever since. No eruption has been recorded here, and Thiên Xu means to keep it that way.
places.art_brief: A natural site, no roofline: a bare black volcanic cone with a wide glowing red-orange mouth at its top, thin smoke rising, cooled lava rivulets with a dull metallic sheen down its flanks, and a ring of small carved grey stone pillars around its lower slope. Grey scree and sparse dry grass at the base. Warm golden light from the top left, the red glow strongest in the mouth. No text, no people, nothing outside the place's footprint.

places.name: Phượng Minh Cung
places.look: High on the ridges of Thê Ngô Lĩnh, a palace of red-lacquered halls and stacked golden-brown pagoda roofs climbs around one colossal ancient wutong (ngô đồng) tree, whose broad green crown rises above the highest roof. Wutong groves fill the terraces below.
places.lore: Phượng Minh Cung, the Palace of the Phoenix's Call, is the great sect of fire and wood in the south, founded on the empty lands of the fallen Cửu Thiều Cung. It holds the rice plain of Triêu Dương Nguyên, whose granaries carried the south through the drought of 649, and since 590 the fire coast of Đan Huyệt Châu. Its head is Hoa Triêu Dương, with the first elder Vu Ngô Đồng at her side. The palace keeps the old court music of the ridges in its rites, but its elders grow uneasy when any tune is played too long, and there are whispers that the palace keeps something of Cửu Thiều's that it never shows.
places.history: Ngô Thê Đồng founded Phượng Minh Cung in 480 on the lands left empty since the fall of Cửu Thiều Cung, and in 485 a market of the Shao music opened at the foot of the new palace. In 520 the palace took the rice plain of Triêu Dương Nguyên, and in the decades after it founded Lai Nghi Thành and its gulf port Thanh Khê Thành. In 584 it asked the Pivot for a writ against Xích Thành Môn, which had burned eleven villages, and won the first writ of the Compact; in 590 it destroyed that sect, took Đan Huyệt Châu and hung the Xích Hà Kỳ in its hall. It fought Băng Tâm Các over the Desert Road from 722 and broke Cô Thành in 726, until the Pivot imposed a truce in 728. In 1040 it went to war with Thính Vũ Lâu for the Kinh Lôi vein, and in 1046 the Pivot's judgement left the vein with Thính Vũ. Ngô Thê Đồng died in 1100 and Hoa Triêu Dương became head; it is whispered in the palace that the dying founder gave her something with a warning, though no one says what. From 1150 to 1158 the palace held Đan Sơn Mạch against Thính Vũ Lâu, with Thiên Xu at its side from 1154.
places.art_brief: The tallest vertical in its land: a palace climbing a high ridge in terraces of red-lacquered timber halls and stacked golden-brown pagoda roofs, wrapped around one colossal wutong tree whose broad pale-green crown rises above the highest roof. Wutong groves on the lower terraces, grey rock and a winding stair at the base. Warm golden light from the top left making the red lacquer and the tree's crown glow. No text, no people or birds larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A second ring of red halls and a covered music terrace climb the ridge around the great wutong, and a stair of red gates runs down toward Thiều Âm Thị.
A nine-roof pagoda rises beside the tree, nearly as tall as its crown, and the terraces spread along the whole ridge with a wutong planted on every step.
projects: music terrace for the dawn rites

places.name: Trúc Thực Viên
places.look: On a low grassy plain, terraced beds of tall golden bamboo bow under heavy tassels of seed, and between them long swept earthen floors are spread with seed drying in the sun. A plain hall roofed with split bamboo stands at the centre.
places.lore: Trúc Thực Viên, the Garden of the Bamboo Seed, is a minor sect of spirit farmers (linh thực sư) sworn to Phượng Minh Cung, founded in 760 to grow the bamboo seed the phoenix eats; it grows spirit grain and beast feed too, and keeps the coast village of Bích Lãng. Its head Ninh Trúc Thực bred a bamboo that seeds every year instead of once in sixty, and the garden's seed now goes to beast keepers across Phượng Minh's lands. Disciples carry the first seed of every harvest up Cao Cương Phong, in case the phoenix comes.
places.history: The phoenix, the saying goes, eats nothing but the seed of the bamboo, and since its founding Phượng Minh Cung had kept a few wild groves of it for its rites, though they seeded only once in sixty years. In 760 spirit farmers founded Trúc Thực Viên on the plain below the ridges to grow that seed, sworn to Phượng Minh. They added spirit grain and beast feed as the palace's needs grew, and took the coast village of Bích Lãng into their keeping. In 1050 Ninh Trúc Thực became head and bred a bamboo that seeds every year instead of once in sixty. The new seed turned the garden from a shrine into a granary, and beast keepers across the south began to buy from it. In the Cinnabar Vein War a century later its seed and grain fed Phượng Minh's war beasts and its wounded at Thanh Khê.
places.art_brief: A minor sect seat on flat grassland, rising in low terraces: beds of tall golden bamboo bowed with pale seed tassels, long swept brown earthen floors between them dotted with drying seed, a modest two-roof hall roofed in split bamboo at the top terrace. Grass and an irrigation ditch at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the bamboo tassels. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A second terrace of seed bamboo and a woven-bamboo seed store join the garden, and a beast pen of woven bamboo stands at the edge.
A tall three-roof hall of bamboo and red timber rises over the beds, with stepped seed terraces spreading from it like a fan.

places.name: Thiều Âm Thị
places.look: At the foot of Phượng Minh's ridges, a market of bamboo-roofed stalls lines a river among bamboo groves, and every lane is hung with curtains of bamboo flutes and pipes drying on strings, clicking and whistling in the wind. A raised music stage stands over the water.
places.lore: Thiều Âm Thị, the Market of the Shao Music, was opened by Phượng Minh's founder in 485 when he cleared the ridges for the new palace. It sells instruments, strings and lacquered drums, and its players are hired for rites all over the south. In 1195 a musician here played a tune no one taught him and every bird on the ridge fell silent; Phượng Minh's elders paid his passage far away, and players since are asked, politely, to name the teacher of any tune they perform.
places.art_brief: A low market cluster along a river in bamboo forest: bamboo-roofed stalls in narrow lanes with many thin hanging strings of pale bamboo flutes, a small raised timber music stage on piles over the water. Bamboo groves and the river at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the hanging flutes. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A covered market hall of bamboo and a second stage on the far bank join the lanes, with a footbridge between them.
The market is walled with a red gate tower, a drum tower and an instrument-makers' guild hall, and a stone landing takes the river boats.

places.name: Mạch Điền Trấn
places.look: A walled town in flat wheat country where a river meets the gulf, dominated by one tall granary raised on a ring of mushroom-shaped staddle stones, its steep thatched roof the highest thing on the plain. Wheat barges tie up at a timber quay below.
places.lore: Mạch Điền Trấn, Wheat Fields Town, grew around its granary after 530, when its wheat fields were set to feed Phượng Minh's palace. The staddle stones keep out rats and high tides alike, and townsfolk boast that their granary never lost a sack in the hungry years.
places.art_brief: A low town inside a rectangular wall at a river mouth on a flat coast: grey-tile roofs around one tall granary with a steep golden thatched roof raised on a ring of squat mushroom-shaped stones, a timber quay with a barge. Golden wheat fields and the gulf at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the thatch. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A second granary on staddle stones and a stone harbour wall join the town, and the town wall is extended to the quay.
A row of great granaries stands along the harbour, with a granary-master's hall and a drum tower over the gate.

places.name: Thanh Khê Thành
places.look: Phượng Minh's port on the gulf sits where a clear brook runs into the sea, a walled grid of grey roofs around a wide harbour. All along the harbour wall hangs an unbroken row of red lanterns, lit every night, so from far out at sea the city shows as a glowing line on the water.
places.lore: Thanh Khê Thành, Clear Brook City, was founded by Phượng Minh Cung in 560 as its port on the gulf. In the Cinnabar Vein War, in 1157, its harbour sheltered Phượng Minh's wounded and the city's lanterns burned all year; the custom stayed, and each family keeps one lantern on the harbour wall lit from dusk to dawn, for those who came home and those who did not. Its brook water is so clear that sailors fill their casks here before any long voyage.
places.history: Phượng Minh Cung founded Thanh Khê Thành in 560 as its port on the gulf, where a clear brook runs into the sea. In its first two centuries it shipped the palace's rice and wheat along the coast and drew in the trade of the south. When Thôn Hải Môn's pirates burned the pearl harbour Châu Lệ Cảng two centuries after the founding, Thanh Khê armed its boats and watched its harbour mouth by night. Soon after, Phượng Minh's fleet sailed in the Pirate Purge under the Pivot's writ, and the Purge ended at Thôn Hải Môn itself. When Thính Vũ Lâu attacked Đan Sơn Mạch and the war dragged on, the harbour became the palace's place of healing. In 1157 it sheltered Phượng Minh's wounded, and the city's lanterns burned all year; they are lit still.
places.art_brief: A walled port city in a rectangular wall where a clear blue brook meets a calm gulf: a grid of grey-tile roofs around a wide harbour, the harbour wall lined along its whole length with a continuous row of small glowing red lanterns, a few boats at anchor. Water and a sandy shore at the base. Warm golden light from the top left, the lanterns glowing softly against the dusk side. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A second wall takes in shipyards along the brook, and a stone harbour arm doubles the anchorage under the lanterns.
A red gate tower stands at the harbour mouth, a three-roof harbour hall faces the gulf, and the lantern row runs round the whole enlarged harbour.

places.name: Đào Khê Thôn
places.look: A small village beside a brook below the ridges, built at the edge of a wide terraced stone platform where wild peach trees grow straight out of the cracks between old paving slabs. Broken stone column bases stand in rows among the trees.
places.lore: Since 400, when wild peach trees grew over the empty palace grounds of the fallen Cửu Thiều Cung and gave the brook below its name, Đào Khê has lived beside the ruin. Villagers pick the peaches but will not cut a tree or lift a paving stone, and nobody sings in the orchard; the dead of the old palace lie in the hills nearby, and grief, the old people say, is still in the ground.
places.art_brief: A low cluster of grey-tile cottages by a brook beside a broad stepped platform of old cracked grey paving, wild pink-flowering peach trees growing out of the cracks, rows of broken stone column bases among them. Grass and the brook at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the peach blossom. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A shrine to the dead of the old palace stands at the orchard's edge, and a peach-drying yard and a small inn join the village.
A walled village of peach farmers and wine makers spreads along the brook, with a gate pavilion facing the ruined platform, on which it never builds.

places.name: Hà Loan Thôn
places.look: A village on a wide river bend, every house raised high on timber stilts above the floodplain and joined by plank walks. Boats are tied under the houses, ready for autumn.
places.lore: The river bend at Hà Loan has flooded every autumn since at least 700, so its people build their houses on stilts. When the water comes the village simply moves into its boats, and the flood is a market season: traders row from house to house selling under the eaves.
places.art_brief: A low cluster of grey-tile houses raised on tall timber stilts on a wide green river bend, thin plank walks between them, small boats tied below. Floodplain grass and the river at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the stilts. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A raised granary and a shrine on a stone mound join the stilt houses, and an earth dike begins along the bend.
A long earthen dike rings the bend, and a small walled market on a raised platform stands among the stilt houses.

places.name: Bích Lãng Thôn
places.look: A fishing village lying just below the level of the gulf behind a seawall of great woven bamboo baskets packed with stones, stacked in a long curve. Bamboo groves crowd the houses, and jade-green waves break against the baskets.
places.lore: Bích Lãng Thôn, Jade Waves Village, fishes the gulf, and its boatmen have long said the jade-green waves carry the fishing boats home. The village lies below the sea and lives by its basket wall, re-woven every winter from Trúc Thực Viên's bamboo; the garden keeps the village, and the village gives the garden fish meal for its beasts.
places.art_brief: A low cluster of grey-tile cottages among bamboo groves on a coast, lying slightly below a long curved seawall made of large stacked woven bamboo baskets filled with stones, jade-green waves breaking on the seaward side, small boats beached inside. Green water at the base. Warm golden light from the top left on the woven baskets. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.
levels: A second ring of baskets and a stone sluice gate guard the village, and a fish-drying yard opens on the wall.
The basket wall is faced with stone and topped by a walk, and a small walled harbour with a shrine to the waves stands at its end.

places.name: Tương Phi Đảo
places.look: A small steep island off the coast, covered from shore to crown in dense bamboo whose canes are flecked with purple-brown spots, like old tear stains. There is no landing and no roof; the bamboo comes right down to the rocks.
places.lore: The spotted bamboo on Tương Phi Đảo, the Isle of the Xiang Consorts, is said to be stained by the tears of two consorts mourning their lord, as in the old legend. Phượng Minh forbids cutting it, and boatmen passing at dusk fall silent out of respect. Flutes of the spotted bamboo made before the ban are said to play sadder than any other.
places.history: The island stood in the gulf long before any sect came south, and the coast people cut its spotted bamboo for flutes and brushes. In the Age of Seven Seats the legend took hold that the spots were the tears of two consorts mourning their lord, and pilgrims began to sail out to see them. In 500 Phượng Minh Cung, newly risen on the ridges, forbade cutting the bamboo. The island has never been settled or claimed, and Phượng Minh keeps its ban by custom rather than by holding the land. The instrument makers of Thiều Âm Thị treasure the old flutes made before the ban and will not sell them lightly. Boatmen of the gulf like to say that the ribs of Thính Vũ Lâu's famous umbrella were cut here long ago, though no one in the Tower has ever said so.
places.art_brief: A natural site, no roofline: a small steep rocky island in jade-green water, covered entirely in dense bamboo whose pale canes are flecked with purple-brown spots, the bamboo crown rounded like a cushion. Dark wet rocks and a ring of white surf at the base, no landing, no buildings. Warm golden light from the top left on the bamboo crown. No text, no people, no boats larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.

places.name: Đan Sơn Mạch
places.look: A steep mountain flank of vermilion rock is split by a long seam that glows a deeper crimson at dusk, where the vein's qi runs close to the surface. Along the ridge above stand the scorched stone footings of watch platforms from the last war.
places.lore: Đan Sơn Mạch, the Vein of the Cinnabar Mountain, is Phượng Minh's spirit vein (linh mạch) near its border with the heart, named after the cinnabar mountain of the old classics where the phoenix is born. Thính Vũ Lâu attacked it in 1150 and was beaten in 1158 with Thiên Xu's help; Mạnh Dạ Vũ swore the Pivot would answer for it, and the palace has kept a guard on the ridge ever since. Alchemists of the south say cinnabar from the seam needs no grinding.
places.history: Cinnabar and silver had long been dug from the slopes around this mountain, and since the Age of Seven Seats Thiên Xu has struck coin from the silver at Bạch Ngân below it. In 900 Phượng Minh found the vein near its border with the heart and named it Đan Sơn Mạch, after the cinnabar mountain where the phoenix is born. The palace guarded it closely, for a vein so near another sect's border was exactly what the Age of Vein Wars was fought over. In 1150 Thính Vũ Lâu attacked Đan Sơn Mạch. In 1154 Doãn Ngọc Hành brought Thiên Xu Tông into the war on Phượng Minh's side, to enforce the Compact. In 1158 Thính Vũ Lâu was beaten at Đan Sơn Mạch and withdrew, and Mạnh Dạ Vũ swore the Pivot would answer for it. The watch platforms burned in the fighting still stand in ruin on the ridge, and the palace has not left the vein unguarded since.
places.art_brief: A natural site, no roofline: a steep vermilion rock mountain flank seen at an angle, split by one long seam glowing deep crimson, a few small scorched grey stone footings of ruined watch platforms along the ridge above. Red scree and sparse dark pines at the base. Warm golden light from the top left deepening the reds. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.

places.name: Cao Cương Phong
places.look: A high bare ridge-top above the wutong hills ends in a flat crest of pale gold stone that takes the first light of dawn before anything else in the south. A single stone pillar stands on the crest, worn at its top into the shape of a perch.
places.lore: Cao Cương Phong, the Peak of the High Ridge, takes its name from the old ode in which the phoenix sings on that high ridge, and it is a sacred summit where the light gathers. Phượng Minh's disciples have climbed it at dawn since at least 600 and say the phoenix sang there. Pilgrims leave nothing on the crest, and what is left anyway is gone by the next dawn.
places.history: It is said that the court musicians of Cửu Thiều Cung named this crest after the ode of the phoenix singing on the high ridge, and played their dawn tunes toward it. After Cửu Thiều fell in the War of the Nine Shao the ridge went quiet for well over a century. When Phượng Minh Cung rose on the empty lands, its disciples took up the dawn climb. By 600 they said the phoenix had sung there, on that high ridge, and the climb became a rite of the palace. Light gathers on the crest at dawn more than anywhere else in the south, and cultivators of light come from far away to sit on it. No sect holds it; Phượng Minh says no one can hold a place the phoenix chose.
places.art_brief: A natural site, no roofline: a tall bare ridge-top rising above green hills, ending in a flat crest of pale gold stone with a single slender stone pillar on it, its top worn into a curved perch. Light scree and a few wind-bent wutong trees at the base. Strong warm golden light from the top left making the crest glow brighter than everything around it. No text, no people, no birds larger than specks, nothing outside the place's footprint.

places.name: Huyền Viên Lâm
places.look: A dense jungle below the wutong hills, where huge strangler figs rise above the canopy, their crowns knotted with the dark apes' woven sleeping platforms of branch and vine. Calls and crashing branches carry from inside, but nothing shows at the edge.
places.lore: Huyền Viên Lâm, the Dark Ape Forest, is held by no sect but by its dark apes, clever black-furred beasts that throw stones and remember faces. Herb gatherers go in only in the morning and leave fruit at the edge; those who do not, the villages say, find their way out blocked by fallen trees.
places.history: The jungle below Thê Ngô Lĩnh's wutong hills has belonged to the dark apes for as long as anyone has kept records. When Cửu Thiều Cung held the ridges, its musicians liked to say the apes sat silent at the jungle's edge to hear the palace's music.
